ledger.note: c. 1243: Mang Kun, a delegate of King Mangrai, founds Kengtung ('Tai Khuen City'). 'Founded around 1243 by a prince named Mang Kun'; the Wa people 'were displaced around 1229'; the Chinese list dates Mang Kun to 1263, and the infobox gives the dynasty's establishment as '3 May' with no year.

ledger.note: 1802: Kengtung under Chiang Mai. 'In 1802 Kengtung came under the rule of Chiang Mai.' The chiangmai dossier carries the same pair as a vassal (1802-1813).

ledger.note: 1814: the Kengtung dynasty is restored with Burmese help and Mongyawng annexed. The page: 'the former dynasty was restored in 1814, with Burmese help'; the chiangmai dossier's page has Maha Hkanan accepting Burmese suzerainty in 1813.

region.text: Kengtung and its substates (Hsenyawt, Hsenmawng, Monghsat, Mongpu): the Shan state east of the Salween, 31,079 km2 in 1901

ledger.note: 1895: the state is counted as ended. The lead says the Shan state 'existed from 1243 to 1895'; the page does not say what happened in 1895 and its saophas ruled until the abdication of 1959. Cliopatria's British Raj shape covers the area from 1885.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1849-1855)
wars.outcome: Kengtung-Konbaung victory: Lanna forces (1850) and Bangkok armies (1852-54) laid siege to Kengtung on 10 March 1853, retreated on 23 March 1853, and withdrew again in March 1854; Siam gained neither Kengtung nor Chiang Hung.
wars.note: No ground was held, so no contest event; the page's infobox territorial result is empty.

certainty.note: The only dimensions are the 1901 area and the substates' names; no frontier is given.

notes: State Cliopatria lacks (its Shan States row 1294-1563 holds it in a ring; konbaung-dynasty, burma and british-raj shapes cover the same cells, so the renderer will see overlaps with those states, which treat it as direct land while pages call it a vassal state). Named by first-toungoo-empire (vassal pair 1562-12 to 1597, counterpart 'Kengtung') and chiangmai (1802-1813, 'kengtung'). Two pages opened. Not settled: (1) the founding year (1243 on the lead; 1263 in the Chinese list) and the end (1895 on the lead, 1959 in the infobox: the saophas continued until 1959 and the Japanese-backed Thai Phayap Army occupied the state from 27 May 1942 until 1945, formalised 1 August 1943; these are not drawn); (2) the page lists the Ming tusi designation of 1405, the Toungoo suzerainty (1562-1597) and the Qianlong-Burma war of 1760 without territorial detail; (3) 'Mongyawng was annexed' in 1814 is not located on any page; (4) the saopha tables disagree, so no ruler strip; (5) gazetteer: the town Kengtung (Chiang Tung, 21.29 N 99.60 E) is not a gazetteer place; the state is drawn by coordinate (100 km). The shape stays through the 1562-1597 Toungoo vassalage and the 1886 British annexation of the Shan states, which the page does not describe.
